sources.title: Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 1,235 flaws, Outlook zero-day

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Windows 11 KB5132061 & KB5131087 cumulative updates released

stories.headline: Microsoft patches a record 1,235 flaws, including Outlook zero-day
stories.dek: November's Patch Tuesday also ships Windows 11 cumulative updates with a customizable context menu, Cloud rebuild and an Xbox mode refresh.
stories.body:
Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes a record 1,235 security flaws, according to BleepingComputer. One of them is a Microsoft Outlook zero-day that is already being actively exploited.

BleepingComputer calls the count record-breaking. Details on the Outlook vulnerability, including how attackers are using it, were not part of the initial report. The fact that it is under active exploitation makes Outlook users the first priority.

For Windows 11, Microsoft has released cumulative updates KB5132061 and KB5131087, covering versions 26H2, 25H2, 24H2 and 23H2. BleepingComputer describes the updates as mandatory because they carry the month's security fixes. Users can install them via Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Updates, or download them manually from the Microsoft Update Catalog. This is the eleventh Patch Tuesday release of 2026. It is based on 24H2, so 25H2 and 26H2 get the same fixes.

The updates also add features. File Explorer gets a faster, customizable right-click context menu. Users can toggle built-in commands, choose which app extensions appear and show Cut, Copy and Paste as menu items instead of icons. The Explorer address bar now accepts ~ as a shortcut to the user profile folder. Xbox mode gains a refreshed Gaming Task View with a navigation bar for Exit to Desktop and Power Options.

On the recovery side, a new Cloud rebuild option reinstalls Windows 11 using an image and drivers downloaded from Windows Update, even when Windows cannot start. No USB media is required. Windows recovery can now reuse saved Wi-Fi profiles automatically. Microsoft is also expanding memory integrity (HVCI), which may be switched on during updates on supported PCs, while respecting existing user or admin choices.

Network admins get IPv6 CLAT support for Wi-Fi and Ethernet, which lets IPv4-only apps reach IPv4 services from IPv6-only networks. Windows Subsystem for Linux and DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation are not currently supported.
key_points: Record 1,235 flaws fixed in November 2026 Patch Tuesday
Outlook zero-day is actively exploited
KB5132061 and KB5131087 cover Windows 11 26H2, 25H2, 24H2 and 23H2
New context menu, Cloud rebuild, Xbox mode Gaming Task View
stories.why_it_matters: An exploited Outlook bug means patching now, not later. Gamers should also note that memory integrity (HVCI) may be switched on during this update on supported PCs.

cover.caption: Security flaws fixed in a record Patch Tuesday

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Customer Datasets, Model Weights and Notion AI Chats

stories.headline: Fireworks AI breach widens to model weights, datasets and Notion chats
stories.dek: A second intrusion through a third-party cloud host exposed billing data, incomplete model weights and Notion AI transcripts, the inference provider says.
stories.body:
Fireworks AI says the security incident it first disclosed in October was broader than it reported at the time. A follow-up investigation found further malicious activity affecting account and billing information, secrets, datasets and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts," The Hacker News reports. Notion, a Fireworks customer, says Notion AI chat transcripts were caught up in it.

In its October 10 notice, Fireworks said it detected unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6. The attacker reached environment variables used in evaluation jobs, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, in some customer accounts. The company said then that it saw no sign that models, datasets, training data, inference traffic or personal information were accessed.

The new bulletin changes that picture. Fireworks says attackers got into an unnamed third-party cloud provider hosting its research and development machines on October 23. On October 24 they used that access to reach Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload that "led to additional customer data impact." Exposed data includes resource metadata, billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balances, credit usage, and a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets. Fireworks says it does not store payment card numbers and has seen no further successful access to its customer platform since October 25.

The company links the attack to a financially motivated cybercriminal group that sells stolen LLM access to illicit routing gateways, a practice known as LLMjacking. Victims are left paying the bill. Google warned last week that LLMjacking attacks on AI infrastructure are rising across several regions and industries.

The downstream effect shows up at Notion. It says fewer than 1 percent of workspaces were affected. It first believed only synthetic testing data was taken, then found Notion AI chat transcripts used for its Insights feature. Most were unattributable, with no author or workspace labels and no tool call results. Notion has disabled Insights and stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

It remains unclear which other Fireworks customers were affected. Notion advises users who pasted passwords, API keys or other credentials into chats during the attack window to rotate them immediately.
key_points: Attackers reached Fireworks dev machines via a third-party cloud host on October 24
Billing data, metadata, incomplete model weights and datasets exposed for some accounts
Notion says fewer than 1% of workspaces hit; AI chat transcripts exposed
Fireworks links the attack to a financially motivated LLMjacking group
stories.why_it_matters: Secrets, datasets and fine-tuned weights sent to an inference provider share that provider's security posture. Anyone using Fireworks keys or pasting credentials into AI chats should rotate them now.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Critical Xen Orchestra auth bypass flaw exploited to hijack VM servers

stories.headline: Attackers exploit Xen Orchestra auth bypass to seize admin access
stories.dek: Vates urges admins to update now: a crafted cookie grants Admin rights and can lead to root takeover of XCP-ng hosts.
stories.body:
Vates is warning that a critical authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra, its web tool for managing XCP-ng virtualization, is being actively exploited, The Hacker News and BleepingComputer report. Tracked as VSA-2026-062 and still without a CVE, the flaw lets an attacker send a cookie containing an empty JSON object and get logged in as the owner of an existing token, with Admin privileges. Vates says that can end in code execution on managed pools and full root takeover of XCP-ng nodes.

Fixes ship in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest), with xo-server 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. It is unclear when attacks began or whether the bug was exploited as a zero-day.

Indicators include a VM named pivot2 and files such as /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar. Vates says exploitation leaves no log traces, so detection requires HTTP monitoring. Compromised users should rotate all passwords and secrets.
key_points: Vates says VSA-2026-062 lets a crafted authenticationToken cookie bypass login with Admin rights, enabling root takeover of XCP-ng hosts.
Patched in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 (xo-server 5.211.2 and 5.213.1); if patching must wait, keep instances off the internet and block the empty token at a WAF or proxy.
Attacks are tied to 91.211.251.112:8001 and a Tor domain; Filip Magic and Christoffer Olsen of TDC NET Security found the flaw.

sources.title: AMD VP and chief Zen architect rebuke claims that Nvidia and Arm made CPUs for agentic AI — ‘We didn’t magically know four years ago that agentic was going to be a thing’

stories.headline: AMD launches Zen 6 EPYC Venice with up to 256 cores per chip
stories.dek: Tom's Hardware's first tests show a 93 percent throughput gain, as AMD's architects dismiss rivals' claims of CPUs built for agentic AI.
stories.body:
AMD has launched EPYC Venice, the first chips on its Zen 6 architecture. In Tom's Hardware's testing, a dual-socket server with two 256-core EPYC 9996 chips and 1,024 threads came out 93 percent ahead of a 2P EPYC 9965 system in SPEC CPU 2026 intrate. The frequency-optimized EPYC 9686F competes directly with Nvidia's Vera.

Zen 6 is built on TSMC's N2P. AMD claims a 27 percent average IPC gain in enterprise, cloud and AI workloads. CCDs grow to 12 cores, or 32 for Zen 6c. Dual I/O dies bring 16 memory channels and PCIe 6.0.

AMD's chief Zen architect Mike Clark and VP Madhu Rangarajan pushed back on Nvidia and Arm marketing "agentic" CPUs. "We didn't magically know four years ago that agentic was going to be a thing," Rangarajan said.
key_points: A 2P EPYC 9996 server beat a 2P EPYC 9965 by 93 percent in SPEC CPU 2026 intrate, per Tom's Hardware.
Zen 6 uses TSMC N2P; AMD claims a 27 percent average IPC uplift over Zen 5 in data center workloads.
Venice-X and the LPDDR5X-based Verano follow next year; consumer Olympic Ridge is also expected next year.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones

stories.headline: Git fixes flaw that runs attacker code on recursive clones
stories.dek: CVE-2026-111760 abuses submodules and hooks; Git 2.56.1 and backports for the 2.50 through 2.55 series close it, along with five other bugs.
stories.body:
The Git project has patched a flaw that lets a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively with its submodules, The Hacker News reports. The fix ships in Git 2.56.1, with backports in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The bug, CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in Git's index handling. An extremely long path passes Git's safety check but is written to disk under a shorter name an attacker can set to .git. That lets the attacker swap a submodule's .git file for a symbolic link to a folder with malicious hooks, which Git then runs.

GitHub has patched github.com and Enterprise Cloud. Git for Windows had not shipped a 2.56.1-based release as of Tuesday, according to The Hacker News. Until you update, avoid recursively cloning untrusted repositories.
key_points: Git 2.56.1 and backported releases fix CVE-2026-111760, which allows code execution during recursive clones with submodules.
The releases also fix five other flaws, including memory corruption in merges and unsafe git fast-import features.
GitHub Enterprise Server fixes are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4; Git for Windows had not yet updated as of Tuesday.

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI

stories.headline: Grok Build share links expose user data, including SpaceXSI's own
stories.dek: Security firm Claroc says a design flaw lets anyone enumerate live Grok Build apps, revealing business plans, medical results and employee IDs.
stories.body:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking sensitive data from thousands of its users, according to research from security firm Claroc reported by Ars Technica. The exposed data includes internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results and employee names and ID numbers.

The leak comes through share links. Grok Build randomizes app URLs, but a design decision makes it possible to enumerate thousands of live projects. Except in rare cases, opening a link reveals all of an app's data. Claroc found 24 apps built by SpaceXSI itself, the merged SpaceX and xAI, exposing a confidential onboarding plan and a sales territory map of 594 accounts.

Claroc says it notified SpaceXSI on Sunday and got no response. After Ars Technica sent questions, the company pulled its own 24 apps. Most other exposed data remained available.
key_points: Claroc says a design flaw lets anyone enumerate live Grok Build share links and view app data.
24 apps built by SpaceXSI exposed internal material, including a 594-account sales territory map.
SpaceXSI removed its own apps after Ars Technica's inquiry; most other exposed data stayed online.

stories.headline: GTA VI tops 10 million pre-orders, MISSIL reports
stories.dek: Swedish outlet MISSIL says Rockstar's long-awaited sequel is now the most pre-ordered game ever, with preloading open ahead of its November 19 launch.
stories.body:
Grand Theft Auto VI has become the most pre-ordered game of all time, according to Swedish gaming site MISSIL. The outlet reports that 10 million pre-orders have been placed, making it the most pre-ordered game product across all categories.

MISSIL also reports that Sony and Microsoft have opened preloading. The companies warn of queues on all servers on launch day, the 19th. MISSIL counted nine days to release when it published on November 10. The outlet says Rockstar has spent 13 years developing the game.

On PS5, Sony's promotional text says the game uses the DualSense controller's speakers, haptics and adaptive triggers, along with Tempest 3D Audio and the console's SSD for faster loading. The game is set in the fictional state of Leonida.
key_points: MISSIL reports 10 million GTA VI pre-orders, a record for any game product.
Sony and Microsoft have opened preloading and expect server queues on launch day, the 19th.
Rockstar has developed the game over 13 years, according to MISSIL.

opinion.headline: Stop waiting for cheap parts and stretch the PC you own
opinion.dek: Chipmakers are chasing data centers and memory is getting pricier, so extend your current platform and upgrade only what your games need.
opinion.body:
AMD reported a record quarter last week: $13.4 billion in revenue, with its data center business doubling and gaming revenue down 40 percent, according to Ars Technica. Days later its CEO called AMD a "data center first" company, a remark TechRadar says makes the priorities clear, with consumers effectively sidelined. Today the first Zen 6 chips arrived. They are EPYC Venice server parts with up to 256 cores each. The consumer version, Olympic Ridge, is expected next year.

Take the company at its word. PC builders who are holding off until prices settle are waiting on a market that no longer puts them first. My advice is to stop planning around a price correction. Stretch the platform you already own, and spend only on the part your actual games are short of.

Plenty of builders have already reached that conclusion. Systems with 64GB of RAM fell 18 percent year over year in CPU-Z's active user base, Tom's Hardware reports, and 32GB setups slipped 2.5 percent. It is the first noticeable decline in higher-capacity configurations the CPU-Z developer has recorded. Meanwhile 16GB configurations rose 12.9 percent and 24GB rose 19.7 percent. DDR4 grew 6 percent to a 54.5 percent share while DDR5 fell 2.9 percent to 32.9 percent. Older Zen 3 chips such as the Ryzen 5 5500 are climbing too. Tom's Hardware blames DDR4 and DDR5 prices pushed up by the AI rush for DRAM supply. These are not people giving up on PC gaming. They are people declining to pay inflated memory prices for a desktop.

Graphics cards face the same pull. Chinese companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation cards this year, Tom's Hardware reports. The same report says a B300 rack that sells for about $600,000 internationally fetched $2.8 million in China last month. Nvidia has also reportedly told cloud partners to keep Chinese customers to 49 percent of their services on new deals, according to the Financial Times, though Nvidia has not confirmed or denied it. If rented capacity gets harder to find, I expect the appetite for cards that can be bought outright to hold. That is a prediction, not a reported fact. But when some buyers will pay more than four times the international price for AI hardware, a gamer is not the only bidder for a gaming card.

The case for waiting deserves a fair hearing. A 40 percent fall in gaming revenue can be read as weak demand, and weak demand usually ends in discounts. The CPU-Z figures reflect systems running CPU-Z, not retail sales, so they may overstate the retreat. Consumer Zen 6 is expected next year, and a new generation normally pushes older parts down in price. And no boom lasts forever.

All of that may be true, and none of it sets a date. A correction requires supply to flow back toward consumers, and the past week's news points the other way: memory is being drawn into AI, the new architecture shipped in servers first, and the company behind it said out loud where desktops rank. What does it cost to be wrong? If prices do fall, the builder who made one targeted upgrade has lost little and can still buy a new platform at the lower price. If they do not, the builder who kept postponing every purchase has put up with a slow machine for nothing.

So measure before spending. Steam's store now shows average frame rates drawn from anonymized data from players with matching hardware, Tom's Hardware reports. Rock Paper Shotgun warns the numbers are not fully trustworthy yet, so treat them as a first check, not a verdict. If the games you play run well on what you have, skip this round. If one component is holding them back, replace that component and nothing else. For memory, follow the crowd in CPU-Z's data: staying on DDR4 and choosing a 16GB or 24GB kit are both legitimate choices, and 64GB is a purchase to justify with a workload, not a habit.

Stretching a platform also means looking after it. AMD says it is fixing a bug in its External Events Utility, a service installed with Radeon drivers that users report writes to SSDs continuously, with one measuring about 5MB/s on an idle PC. PC Gamer could not reproduce it, and a user's claim of losing 1 percent of SSD health a month is unconfirmed. Radeon owners can open Resource Monitor and look for sustained writes from atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe. PC Gamer expects the driver fix later this month.

Watch three things. First, whether Olympic Ridge arrives next year as expected and what it does to the price of older chips. Second, whether 64GB and DDR5 recover in CPU-Z's numbers, which would suggest memory is getting easier to afford. Third, whether AMD's gaming revenue recovers, or the company keeps describing itself the way it did this month. Until one of those moves, buy for the games you play now, not for the market you hope returns.
opinion.pull_quote: Stretch the platform you already own, and spend only on the part your actual games are short of.
opinion.topic: Gaming PCs in a data-center-first market
opinion.thesis: AMD calling itself 'data center first' while gaming revenue falls 40 percent, plus AI-driven memory prices and Chinese firms buying up gaming cards, means PC builders should not wait for a price correction. The smart move is to stretch the platform you already own, as buyers drifting back to DDR4 and smaller kits already are, and upgrade only what your actual games need.
